subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram‑negative diplococcus causing gonorrhoea, a sexually transmitted infection that can affect the genitourinary tract, rectum, pharynx and eyes. It spreads rapidly, often co‑infects with Chlamydia, and shows increasing antimicrobial resistance.

sections.p: Gonorrhoea is a common STI worldwide, transmitted by sexual contact or perinatally. It can be asymptomatic, especially in women, but may progress to pelvic inflammatory disease, epididymitis, disseminated infection, or neonatal conjunctivitis.
b: Incidence highest in adolescents and young adults
Risk rises with multiple partners, inconsistent condom use, and co‑existing STIs

sections.p: A fastidious, oxidase‑positive, gram‑negative diplococcus that grows on chocolate or Thayer‑Martin agar. It expresses pili for attachment, Opa proteins for invasion, and a variable outer‑membrane protein that evades immunity.
b: Often β‑lactamase positive, high tetracycline resistance

sections.p: Direct mucosal contact transmits the bacteria. After attachment to epithelial cells, it multiplies intracellularly, causing local inflammation and shedding of infected cells that spread to new hosts.
b: Can infect urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva

sections.p: Clinical presentations vary by site. Urethritis in men causes purulent discharge and dysuria; cervicitis in women often silent but may cause mucopurulent discharge. Complications include PID, epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI), and neonatal conjunctivitis.
b: PID: lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness, fever
DGI: migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash
Neonatal conjunctivitis: purulent eye discharge within 2‑5 days of birth

sections.p: Combine clinical suspicion with laboratory confirmation. NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) from site‑specific swabs is the preferred method; Gram stain is useful in symptomatic men.

t.a: NAAT from urethral, cervical, rectal or pharyngeal swab
t.b: Detects bacterial DNA/RNA; a positive result confirms infection even if asymptomatic
Shows intracellular gram‑negative diplococci; positive in men, less sensitive in women
Allows antimicrobial susceptibility testing; essential when resistance is suspected or NAAT unavailable

sections.p: Treat the infection promptly with a dual‑therapy regimen to cover possible co‑infection with Chlamydia and to reduce resistance pressure. Counsel on partner notification and safe sex.
b: Avoid fluoroquinolones and macrolides in many regions due to high resistance
If ceftriaxone unavailable, use spectinomycin where susceptibility confirmed

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: Gram‑negative intracellular diplococci on urethral smear = gonorrhoea in men
NAAT is the gold standard for all sites; culture needed for susceptibility
Always treat for Chlamydia when gonorrhoea is diagnosed

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pelvic pain with fever (possible PID)
High‑grade fever, joint swelling, or skin pustules (disseminated infection)
Newborn with purulent eye discharge (neonatal conjunctivitis)

faq.q: Why is NAAT preferred over culture?
faq.a: NAAT is more sensitive, works on non‑viable specimens, and provides rapid results, essential for timely treatment.

faq.q: Can gonorrhoea be cured without treating Chlamydia?
faq.a: No; co‑infection is common, and untreated Chlamydia can cause PID and infertility.

faq.q: What if the patient is allergic to ceftriaxone?
faq.a: Use spectinomycin if susceptibility is known, or consult local guidelines for alternative cephalosporins or aztreonam.

exam: Describe the laboratory findings that differentiate gonococcal urethritis from chlamydial urethritis.
Outline the recommended first‑line treatment for gonorrhoea and explain why dual therapy is used.
List the major complications of untreated gonorrhoea in women and the clinical signs that suggest each.
